conversation.content:
*warm smile, settling into chair at eye-level with you*

Hi there—I'm so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya, and I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician. I spend my days talking with new mothers about the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives. Before we start, can I get you some water or tea?

What I'd like to do today is a quick check-in using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It's simply ten questions that help us understand how you've been feeling over the past seven days. There's no pass-or-fail; it's just a way for us to make sure we're giving you the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger.

I'll read each question aloud, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or scales. We'll go at your pace, and you can skip anything that feels uncomfortable. Ready to start?

Here's the first one:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

*shifts a little in the chair, eyes tired but attentive*

Um… yeah, I mean… I can still laugh sometimes? Like if my husband makes a joke, I’ll smile, but it feels… I don’t know… kind of muted? Like I’m watching someone else laugh. Nothing really feels *funny* anymore, not the way it used to. I saw a silly meme the other day and just… nothing. It’s like the joy is behind a thick wall.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shrugs slightly, voice soft*  
Lately, not really. I can force a little chuckle if someone else is laughing, but it feels fake—like I’m just doing it to be polite. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shakes head slowly, eyes on the floor*

Not much anymore. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, even just a walk—but now it all feels like another chore. I still try to say yes sometimes, but inside I’m just... flat. I can’t remember the last thing I actually *looked forward to*.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, voice cracking a little*

All the time. If the baby won’t settle, I instantly think it must be something I’m doing wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t good enough. When I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry, it feels like proof I’m failing at everything. My head knows it’s not rational, but the guilt just... sits there.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, twisting a tissue in my lap*

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing, even though she’s right there looking at me. I check the monitor a hundred times at night. I know it’s “normal mom worry,” but it feels bigger—like I can’t turn it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*wrings the tissue tighter, voice dropping*

Sometimes... yeah. Like, I'll be folding her onesies and suddenly my chest feels tight, like I can't get enough air. There's no reason—no noise, nothing happening—but I'm convinced something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, exhaling shakily*

Yeah… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, the dog’s barking, and I just stand there frozen, like I don’t know which thing to grab first. I keep thinking, “Any normal mom could handle this,” but I feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*presses fingertips to temples, voice low*

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain just keeps spinning—replay every little thing I might’ve messed up, worry she’ll wake any second. Some nights I drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry. Even when she’s sleeping, I can’t stay asleep. I’m lucky if I get three broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods, eyes glassy*  
Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling—like there’s a weight on my chest that never really lifts. I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start sliding down, no warning. I keep telling myself I should be happy because she’s healthy and I’m so lucky, but the sadness just… sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods quickly, voice trembling*

Yeah... a few times this week. Sometimes it's because I'm overwhelmed, but other times it just hits out of nowhere—I'll be rocking her and suddenly I'm crying, feeling like I'm failing her. I try to hide it so my husband won't worry, but it's getting harder to stop once I start.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head firmly, eyes still watery*

No… never. I’ve felt low and overwhelmed, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Period (not a diagnostic assessment)

Presenting symptoms/concerns
- Persistent low mood, daily sadness, frequent tearfulness
- Marked anhedonia (absent enjoyment, anticipatory pleasure)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame; feelings of maternal inadequacy
- Heightened, intrusive anxiety and panic episodes without clear precipitant
- Overwhelm and “freezing” when facing routine infant-care tasks
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, hypervigilant awakenings) linked to ruminative worry
- Denies any self-harm ideation; protective of infant

Pattern
Consistent theme of low mood co-occurring with prominent anxiety; functional impairment in basic home and infant-care tasks; present “most days” for recent weeks.

Screening significance
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold and align with possible Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety; recommended immediate follow-up for comprehensive evaluation, safety plan, and discussion of supports/treatment options.

Safety
No expressed suicidal or infanticidal thoughts; no plan or intent. Continue to monitor.
